summary: Light at the mouth of Musquash Harbour west of Saint John: first exhibited 1879, hexagonal concrete tower since 1959, still on the Coast Guard list, now a trail destination.

structures.note: Square wooden tower, forty feet, with an attached keeper's dwelling (LHF). Replaced by the 1959 tower.
LHF gives 47 ft (14.3 m); the Coast Guard list gives a structure height of 14.0 m.

staffing.note: LHF: automated in the early 1980s; the last keeper left in 1987.

access.note: Reached by King William Road, a rough road to a red gate, then a 1.2 km (0.9 mi) walk on a dirt road. Grounds open, tower closed (LHF). Rowlett gives a hike of about 1.5 km (1 mi) round trip, which does not agree.

facts.agency: Nature Conservancy of Canada and Explore Lorneville Inc. (land and trails, 2021); Musquash Head Lightstation Inc. (2008 owner, since disbanded). The light stays on the Canadian Coast Guard's List of Lights.
facts.ownership: disputed: LHF visitor notes name Musquash Head Lightstation Inc. as owner (that company disbanded, per LHF); Rowlett lists the Nature Conservancy of Canada as owner/site manager; the Coast Guard list carries the remark 'Private aid'

events.note: Clockwork replaced by a new Reliance clock (LHF).
Modern revolving apparatus with motor drive and two 900 W generating units (LHF).
Present hexagonal concrete tower built, replacing the 1879 wooden tower (LHF; Rowlett).
Fog horn added after the Tiner Point fog horn was discontinued (LHF).
Ceremony on 21 July 2008 at the New Brunswick Museum: DFO divested the lighthouse to community groups (LHF; Rowlett gives July 2008).
NCC acquired a 92-acre parcel at Musquash Head that includes the lighthouse, through a partnership with Explore Lorneville (reported 1 June 2021).

corrections.why: The light was first exhibited in 1879 (LHF; Rowlett). The 1959 event replaced the tower; it did not first light the station.
LHF says the lighthouse was automated in the early 1980s and the last keeper left in 1987.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata has the light inactive. The Coast Guard list gives it as a white flash every three seconds, so the light is treated as active.
The station's first light is 1879 (LHF; Rowlett). The 1959 date is the present concrete tower, which replaced the wooden one. Both are right for their own structure.
LHF gives 47 ft (14.3 m) for the 1959 tower and the Coast Guard list gives a 14.0 m structure height. Both are kept with their sources; the difference is small and the list is the official figure.
Lighthouse Friends and the Coast Guard list give a hexagonal tower; Rowlett gives an octagonal one. The story states both.

Lighthouse Friends names Musquash Head Lightstation Inc. as owner and also says that company disbanded; Rowlett names the Nature Conservancy of Canada as owner/site manager. Not resolved; the 2021 news reports do not name a titleholder.

notes_for_editor: Most of the history from 1879 to 1987 rests on LighthouseFriends, which cites the Department's annual reports 'various years' without page numbers. The corpus holds the Canadian reports only from 1900, so the 1878 appropriation, the contract, the 1879 first exhibition and the 1880 Split Rock buoy are LHF's account and are not checked against an official record. The keeper tables (reports published 1906 and 1908) confirm Hamm only for those years. The 1912 clockwork and 1929 apparatus lines are LHF only. The 1913-14 improvements list names an 'East Head Musquash' entry, but the OCR separates the names from their descriptions, so that entry is not used. Lighthouse Digest's 2008 divestiture article returned a server error and the CBC 2020 article timed out; neither was read. The Coast Guard list's date-modified stamp is 2026-09-24. The post-1960 keepers (Tiner, Hoar, Wilson) appear with years and role only, as LHF gives them. The record's Wikidata 'deactivated 1959' event is unchecked. Fact-check of 2026-10-28: the buoy distance now reads as Lighthouse Friends gives it (about 1 1/2 miles from the lighthouse, marking Split Rock), not as a distance from Split Rock; the 'volunteer group' attribution and the 'grant' wording (the source says donation) are corrected; the cost lines now follow the LHF figures. Rowlett's disagreements are stated: octagonal tower, a 1.5 km round-trip hike against LHF's 1.2 km walk, and the Nature Conservancy as owner/site manager. The 1906 and 1908 keeper-table rows for Hamm were matched to Musquash by OCR position: the scan pages (p. 341 and p. 149) were not read as images, because the in-app browser refused archive.org during this check, so the page images should be looked at before the keeper line is relied on. The Coast Guard 'Private aid' remark is quoted only; no source explains it.
